title: The real Great Escape — 76 men out of Stalag Luft III, only 3 made it
sources: Wikipedia: Stalag Luft III — a Luftwaffe camp for captured airmen near Sagan (now Żagań, Poland), sited on sandy soil to make tunnelling difficult, with huts raised about 60 cm off the ground so guards could detect tunnelling; Squadron Leader Roger Bushell planned a mass escape through three tunnels, Tom, Dick and Harry; about 600 prisoners worked on them; the tunnels were about 9 m (30 ft) deep and 0.6 m (2 ft) square, shored up with wood from bed boards (4,000 bed boards went missing); an air pump was built from bed parts, hockey sticks, knapsacks and Klim milk tins; sand was scattered from pouches hidden inside trousers; on the night of 24/25 March 1944, 76 men crawled out of Harry before the 77th was spotted at 4:55 a.m.; Leonard Trent VC, who had reached the tree line, surrendered; 73 were recaptured; Hitler wanted all of them shot, and 50 were executed; only three reached freedom — the Norwegians Per Bergsland and Jens Müller (to Sweden by boat) and the Dutchman Bram van der Stok (to Spain); only one American, Johnnie Dodge, took part, despite the 1963 Hollywood film.

Photos (public domain / CC0, Wikimedia Commons, Imperial War Museum): Allied prisoners of war in Germany; prisoners' drawings of Stalag Luft III; the memorial to the Fifty; the line of tunnel Harry at Żagań; Jens Müller with his Hurricane (1941); Leonard Trent (1943); Peter Butterworth's Stalag Luft III POW card

Archive film (public domain): 'Mining and Preparation of Anthracite Coal' (underground tunnels, illustrative); Universal Newsreel 1944-11-22 (RAF Lancaster, German countryside); US Army, 'The 82nd Anniversary of the Great Escape' (Żagań, 2026)
Music: Grieg, In the Hall of the Mountain King, Musopen, public domain

post.facebook:
In March 1944, 76 men crawled out of a Nazi prison camp through a tunnel built from bed boards and tin cans. Only three made it home.

Stalag Luft III held captured Allied airmen and was built on sand so nobody could tunnel out. Squadron Leader Roger Bushell planned three tunnels anyway — Tom, Dick and Harry — and 600 men worked on them: nine metres down, held up with 4,000 boards stolen from their own beds, with an air pump made of hockey sticks and milk tins, and the sand smuggled out in bags hidden inside their trousers.

On a moonless night, 24 March 1944, 76 men crawled through Harry into the forest before number 77 was spotted. 73 were caught, and on Hitler's orders 50 of them were shot by the Gestapo. Only three reached freedom: two Norwegian pilots who reached Sweden by boat, and a Dutch pilot who made it to Spain.

Hollywood later filled the tunnel with Americans — in reality only one American took part. Fifty men died for a few days of freedom. Was it worth it? 👇

youtube.description:
In March 1944, 76 men crawled out of a Nazi prison camp through a tunnel built from bed boards and tin cans. Only three made it home.

The true story behind The Great Escape (1963): Squadron Leader Roger Bushell's plan for three tunnels — Tom, Dick and Harry — under Stalag Luft III at Sagan (now Żagań, Poland). 600 prisoners dug nine metres down through sand, using 4,000 stolen bed boards and a pump made of hockey sticks and Klim milk tins. On 24–25 March 1944, 76 men escaped through Harry; 73 were recaptured and 50 were executed by the Gestapo on Hitler's orders. Only Per Bergsland, Jens Müller and Bram van der Stok reached freedom — and only one American took part.
